newsitem.title: USA: RJR witness says cigarette health risks well known.
newsitem.headline: RJR witness says cigarette health risks well known.

text.p: An expert witness for RJR Nabisco Holding Corp's R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co played a recording of an old Tex Williams song and recalled cigarette nicknames like "coffin nails" Tuesday to show that the health risks of smoking have been part of common public knowledge for a long time.

Using a multimedia presentation that included snippets of old news broadcasts and the 1947 smoking song "Smoke, Smoke, Smoke That Cigarette," University of South Carolina historian Lacy Ford told jurors in a wrongful death trial that there was substantial publicity on the possible links between smoking and illness from the early 1900s through the 1960s.
Lawyers for Reynolds, appeared to be using the testimony to bolster their claim that the late Jean Connor chose to smoke despite knowing the possible health risks.

Connor, who smoked from the time she was a teen-ager and eventually developed a three-pack-a-day habit, died of lung cancer at age 49. Her sister, Dana Raulerson, sued Reynolds for wrongful death on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children.

The smoking song, written in 1947 by Merle Travis for Tex Williams, includes the lyrics "puff, puff, puff until you smoke yourself to death," and "nicotine slaves are all the same, at a petting party or a poker game."
Williams was a heavy smoker who died in 1985 following a yearlong battle with cancer.

Defense lawyers played a segment of a CBS News Extra report moderated by Harry Reasoner on the 1964 U.S. Surgeon-General's report that linked smoking with lung ailments. In it, Reasoner said: "If you smoke cigarettes, you increase your chances of dying early."
"This was really just saturation coverage" of the Surgeon-General's report, Ford said, comparing the media reporting to that of the O.J. Simpson murder saga.
He said the public was aware not only of the possible health risk, but also of the allegedly addictive nature of cigarettes.
There was a "broad public awareness amounting to common knowledge of those facts for a very long time," Ford said.

Ford, who said he did not read medical journals or internal tobacco company documents to form his perceptions on common knowledge about smoking, cited a 1954 Gallup Poll in which 90 percent of those questioned had heard or read that smoking may cause lung cancer.
